headline: Neuromorphic edge AI IP licensing model: upfront license fees plus royalties on chip ASP, with first royalty revenues expected within ~18 months from Edge AI Inc deal
reasoning: BrainChip designs neuromorphic computing IP for customers who build their own chips, charging an upfront license fee and then a royalty as a percentage of average selling price once customer chips reach production. The Edge AI Inc licence is expected to move to production in roughly 18 months or less. A separate channel arrangement with Asit Glan (ALAN) involves pre-purchased trial licences that convert to full licences and royalties if a customer proceeds to full chip production, which could take a couple of years beyond that. BrainChip also participates in Intel's foundry IP library as a certified partner. The company does not own fabs and works with third-party foundries to manufacture its own Akita silicon chips.
quote: Sure, it's two different kind of relationships. You know, it's interesting. Edge AI is the name of a company as well as a category. We're talking, but in that case, it's a classic customer. They take it, they design their chip. And once that chip comes out and they and they test it and make sure it works, then they go to production and then they start to ship it. So the way it works is when they buy a license from us, we get a fee, you know, a a very expensive fee, because that's what IP costs across the entire industry. And then when their chips come out, it's very typical. A royalty, a small percentage of the ASP average sales price of chips would come from us. So, you know, depending on how fast somebody can go to chips, sometimes that could take years. In this case it's probably, um, less, less than two, you know, maybe a year and a half. So so that one's we're expecting pretty quickly to go relatively quick.

headline: Strong secular shift toward edge AI across all verticals — defence, wearables, industrial IoT and oil & gas — driven by power efficiency, latency and security needs
reasoning: Sean Hehir argues that AI deployment is following a historical computing pattern of centralisation (data centre) followed by decentralisation (edge), and that this shift is now well underway across every industry vertical. Defence is highlighted as particularly hot given the move from fixed positions to mobile platforms like drones and robots. Wearables and industrial IoT are also called out as key growth vectors. Neuromorphic computing is positioned as the most power-efficient approach for edge AI, making it well-suited to battery-constrained devices.
quote: Yeah. So you know what's interesting about edge high. It's affecting literally all segments across the entire economy. Anything that requires battery power and mobility requires. So some of the more specific verticals we're seeing are things around defense. Of course, the nature of the world today, defense has changed from kind of large fixed positions to more mobile things like drones and robots. Of course, you need edge computing for those kind of things. So defense is a very hot market for that. Uh, wearable devices, things that you wear on your face and your wrist. If you want to do edge computing, you want to make sure you do it with a very power efficient technology, because you don't want to have to charge it all the time. Industrial IoT, because, you know, preventive maintenance signature. We work with oil and gas companies. So it's virtually every single industry across the globe right now is all pushing towards greater productivity and adding greater feature and function to end products with edge AI.

headline: New Sakura product class targets generative AI at the edge using SSMs, with leadership position claimed on memory innovation and model distillation
reasoning: Sean Hehir describes Brainchip's new Sakura product class as a significant extension beyond the existing Akita line, targeting generative AI workloads at the edge. The company is betting heavily on state space models (SSMs) over transformers, arguing SSMs will outperform in the long run. Brainchip has developed its own proprietary SSM class and offers customers a turnkey solution combining the accelerating hardware and the models themselves. Hehir claims a 'very strong and defensible leadership position' given the firm's deep history in model acceleration and innovative approaches to memory usage and model distillation.
quote: Yeah, of course others are trying. I feel very comfortable saying we're coming out of the gate with a very strong leadership position. Brain Chip has the best scientists and engineers in the world. We have a history of doing nothing but accelerating models. That's what this company does. Um, so we are we've got some very innovative approaches to do this without turning this very, very technical. Um, but we've got some very innovative approaches around the use of memory particularly, and the ability to distill models that are very innovative. And then, of course, we're leaning very hard into a new kind of class of models called SSM or state space models. So Cora will support Transformers and SSMs, but we believe strongly that SSMs will outperform it in the long run.
